1: King Ahasuerus of Persia holds a lavish feast. Queen Vashti refuses to be displayed and loses her crown.
A proud court sets the scene.
2: Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, is chosen as queen and keeps her people secret. Mordecai uncovers a plot against the king.
God places people where they will be needed.
3: The official Haman is furious that Mordecai will not bow to him. He obtains a decree to destroy all Jews on a day chosen by lot.
4: Mordecai asks Esther to plead with the king. To approach uninvited means death. He says, "Who knows whether you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?"
Our position is given for a purpose.
5: The king receives her, and she invites him and Haman to a banquet. Haman builds a gallows for Mordecai.
6: The sleepless king reads of Mordecai's loyalty and has Haman lead him through the city in royal robes.
The reversal begins, by a sleepless night.
7: At the second banquet Esther reveals she is a Jew and names Haman. He is hanged on his own gallows.
The trap closes on its maker.
8: Mordecai is raised to honour, and the Jews are permitted to defend themselves.
9: The Jews overcome their enemies, and the feast of Purim is established to remember it.
10: Mordecai is second to the king. He recalls a dream of two dragons and a small spring that became a river: the spring was Esther.
God had planned the rescue from the start. From here on the chapters come from the Greek text.
11: Mordecai's dream is told: noise, two dragons ready to fight, and a little fountain that grew into a great river.
What looked small was God's instrument.
12: A fuller account of how Mordecai exposed the plot against the king and how Haman came to hate him.
13: The text of Haman's decree. Mordecai prays, explaining that he refused to bow so as not to give a man God's honour.
14: Esther lays aside her royal robes and prays: "Help me, who am alone and have no helper but you."
The prayer of someone facing danger with no one but God.
15: Esther approaches the throne in fear and faints. God changes the king's spirit to gentleness.
God holds the hearts of rulers.
16: The decree in favour of the Jews: Haman is condemned, and the Jews are declared just and children of the living God.
A pagan king ends by acknowledging God.
